note: Every fact checked on the NSSDCA Phoenix page (challenge catalogue) and NASA's Phoenix mission page.

facts.text: Phoenix launched on 4 August 2007 on a Delta II from Cape Canaveral. The 681 million km cruise to Mars took about 10 months.
facts.sourceName: NASA NSSDCA: Phoenix Mars Lander (challenge catalogue)

facts.text: During descent the parachute opened, the heat shield was ejected 15 seconds later and the legs deployed 10 seconds after that. At 1 km the parachute was released and 8 pulsed thrusters made a soft landing, turning off when footpad sensors felt touchdown.
facts.sourceName: NASA NSSDCA: Phoenix Mars Lander (challenge catalogue)

facts.text: Phoenix landed on 25 May 2008 at 23:53:44 UT, at 68.22 degrees north on the arctic plains of Mars (Vastitas Borealis), farther north than any previous mission: a latitude like northern Alaska.
At touchdown Mars was 275 million km from Earth, a light travel time of about 15 minutes.
facts.sourceName: NASA NSSDCA: Phoenix Mars Lander (challenge catalogue)

facts.text: The lander waited 15 minutes for the dust to settle before unfurling its solar panels. The first images showed a flat surface with pebbles and troughs, but no large rocks or hills.
Phoenix had an octagonal base on three landing legs, with two octagonal solar panel wings for power. Its science payload had a mass of 55 kg.
facts.sourceName: NASA NSSDCA: Phoenix Mars Lander (challenge catalogue)

facts.text: Within four days Phoenix sent a full 360-degree panorama, deployed its 2.5 m robotic arm and started returning weather reports. Its stereo camera stood on a 2 m mast.
Phoenix studied the history of water in the Martian arctic, where water ice is found, and searched for complex organic molecules.

On 31 May the robotic arm began sampling the soil for ice. By 19 June scientists concluded that bright clumps in the Dodo-Goldilocks trench were probably water ice: they vaporized four days after being scooped.
Phoenix carried tiny ovens (TEGA) that heated soil samples. On 31 July NASA announced that there is water on Mars, based on a sample analyzed by TEGA.

On 5 August the team announced perchlorates in the soil: a possible energy source for microbes and a potentially valuable resource for human explorers, which neither confirmed nor refuted the possibility of life.

The wet chemistry laboratory (MECA) mixed water brought from Earth with the soil. Early results suggested the soil was alkaline, with salts such as perchlorate, sodium, magnesium, chloride and potassium.
At 68 degrees north the Sun stayed in the sky all the time after landing and did not dip below the horizon until August.
facts.sourceName: NASA NSSDCA: Phoenix Mars Lander (challenge catalogue)

facts.text: By the end of August Phoenix had completed its planned 90-day mission, which was extended to 30 September.
As the summer ended Phoenix had less solar energy, and it made its last transmission on 2 November 2008 before its power was depleted.
facts.sourceName: NASA NSSDCA: Phoenix Mars Lander (challenge catalogue)

facts.text: From landing on 25 May 2008 to the last signal on 2 November 2008 is 161 days (our count from the two dates).
facts.sourceName: NASA NSSDCA: Phoenix Mars Lander (challenge catalogue)
